ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Probing of Large Language Models with Embedding Analysis
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of embedding analysis techniques, such as diffusion maps and trajectory analysis, to reduce the dimensionality of the high-dimensional internal state of LLMs. This will enable the detection of informative layers and tokens without the need for exhaustive probing of all internal states, making the approach more efficient and scalable.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to traditional non-dynamic embedding analysis, as well as a baseline that exhaustively probes the entire internal state of the LLM.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should be significantly faster than exhaustive probing while maintaining a high level of accuracy, especially in regions with dense, informative clusters of points. However, it may struggle with LLMs that exhibit unusual or anomalous behavior, leading to sparse or heterogeneous patterns in the embedding space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Layer-Specific and Token-Specific Representations in Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We will use the framework of representation learning to investigate the relationship between layer-specific and token-specific representations of the internal state of LLMs and the occurrence of hallucinations. Specifically, we will examine whether a detector can be trained to identify specific layers or tokens that are indicative of hallucinations, and whether this can be used to improve detection accuracy.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to those of efficient probing, as well as a baseline that uses a fixed, layer-specific probing location.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should show that layer-specific and token-specific representations are informative for hallucination detection, and that using both can lead to improved accuracy. However, we may find that the optimal layers or tokens vary depending on the specific LLM and task, making it challenging to develop a universally applicable detector.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Layer-Specific and Token-Specific Representations in Hallucination Detection
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will extend our previous proposal by investigating the use of attention weights as an additional feature for hallucination detection. Specifically, we will examine whether the attention weights assigned to different layers or tokens can provide additional information about the presence of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to those of efficient probing, as well as a baseline that uses a fixed, layer-specific probing location, and a baseline that does not use attention weights.
COST: 750 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should show that incorporating attention weights provides additional information about hallucinations, leading to improved detection accuracy. However, we may find that the optimal way to incorporate attention weights varies depending on the specific LLM and task, requiring additional hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Efficient Probing of Large Language Models with Embedding Analysis
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will add a dimensionality reduction step to the existing embedding analysis approach to further reduce the dimensionality of the internal state of LLMs. This will enable the utilization of more efficient and scalable techniques like sparse linear probing or even a sparse k-NN probe to extract hallucination-related information.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to traditional non-dynamic embedding analysis, as well as a baseline that exhaustively probes the entire internal state of the LLM, and a baseline that uses a fixed, layer-specific probing location.
CONTROLS-ADD: We will also investigate the effect of varying the dimensionality reduction approach on the quality of hallucination detection.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should lead to a substantial decrease in computational costs for hallucination detection while maintaining or improving the accuracy, depending on the chosen dimensionality reduction method and its complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Transferable Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We will explore adversarial training as a method to improve the transferability of hallucination detection across different LLMs and tasks. Specifically, we will use a generator-network to produce fabricated hallucinations for a given LLM-task pair, and train the hallucination detector to distinguish between real and fabricated hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that trains the hallucination detector on seen LLMs and tasks only, as well as to a baseline that uses a domain adaptation approach.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should show that adversarial training improves the transferability of hallucination detection across LLMs and tasks, but may require careful tuning of the generator-network and detector to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leveraging Structural Similarity for Cross-Model Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of structural similarity measures (e.g., correlation, cosine similarity) to transfer hallucination knowledge from one LLM to another. Specifically, we will train a hallucination detector on the internal state of one LLM (source model) and then fine-tune it on the internal state of another LLM (target model) using structural similarity measures to align the internal representations of the two models.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that trains the hallucination detector from scratch on the target model, as well as to a baseline that uses a domain adaptation approach.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should show that leveraging structural similarity improves the cross-model hallucination detection accuracy, but may require careful selection of structural similarity measures and hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Real-World Hallucination Detection with Model-Agnostic Deep Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We will design and train a model-agnostic deep neural network (DNN) to detect hallucinations in real-world scenarios. Specifically, we will use a pre-trained DNN and fine-tune it on a dataset of LLM-generated text with manually annotated hallucinations. To make the detector scalable, we will integrate it with a probabilistic sampling strategy that prioritizes instances with high hallucination uncertainty.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that uses a pre-trained LLM-specific hallucination detector, as well as to a baseline that trains a new DNN from scratch.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should show that the model-agnostic DNN provides highly competitive hallucination detection accuracy while requiring minimal fine-tuning, making it a scalable and practical solution for real-world applications.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Scalable Real-World Hallucination Detection with Model-Agnostic Deep Neural Networks
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will extend our previous proposal by incorporating attention and Transformer architectures into the model-agnostic DNN to improve its ability to detect hallucinations in real-world scenarios. We will also evaluate the impact of different attention mechanisms (e.g., multi-head attention, self-attention) on the DNN's performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that uses a pre-trained LLM-specific hallucination detector with attention and Transformer architectures, as well as to a baseline that trains a new DNN from scratch with a different attention mechanism.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should show that the model-agnostic DNN with attention and Transformer architectures provides improved hallucination detection accuracy in real-world scenarios, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hallucination Detection for LLMs in Multitask Scenarios
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the detection of hallucinations in LLMs that are trained for multiple tasks (e.g., question answering, text classification, sentiment analysis). We will propose a method to leverage the relationships between tasks and detect hallucinations that are common across multiple tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to a baseline that trains separate hallucination detectors for each task.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should show that our method can improve hallucination detection accuracy in multitask LLMs by leveraging task relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Hallucination Detection Methods on Real-World Datasets
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the hallucination detection methods proposed in this study on a range of real-world datasets, including movie review sentiment analysis and factual question answering. We will compare the performance of each method and provide recommendations for practical use.
CONTROLS: We will compare our methods to state-of-the-art baselines and ablate different components to understand their contributions.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results should provide a thorough understanding of the performance of different hallucination detection methods on real-world datasets and guide future research in this area.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient LLM Probing with Tokenized Representations
PROPOSAL: Design a detector that uses a learnable, convolutional layer to process the full internal state of an LLM, after tokenizing the activations into a fixed-size matrix. This detector will leverage the benefits of processing the full internal state while minimizing the impact of high dimensionality.
CONTROLS: Linear probing classifier as baseline, ablating the convolutional layer to compare with traditional single-token probing methods.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The detector will outperform traditional single-token probing methods, while being computationally efficient enough for real-world deployment. It may struggle with tasks that require fine-grained control over the processing of the internal state.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-LLM Knowledge Transfer with Shared Linear Latent Spaces
PROPOSAL: Develop a shared linear latent space framework where multiple LLMs share a common, sparse separated representation of factual truth. This framework involves training a set of linear converters to map each LLM's hidden state into this shared space, and then designing a detector that operates on this shared space. This approach aims to facilitate the transfer of knowledge across LLMs.
CONTROLS: Experiments with different sparsity patterns and converter architectures, comparing to a standalone detector trained on a single LLM.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The shared latent space framework will significantly improve the generalization of hallucination detection across different LLMs, while the choice of sparsity pattern may require further exploration to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Exploring Hierarchical LLM Probing with Attention and Tree Structures
PROPOSAL: Revise the detector from proposal 1 to incorporate attention and tree structures, allowing it to selectively focus on the most informative regions of the internal state. The detector will process the full internal state of an LLM in a hierarchical manner, using a combination of attention and tree-based methods to contextually weight the importance of different tokens and layers.
CONTROLS: Comparing with the original tokenized convolutional detector, ablating the attention and tree-based components to understand their contribution.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised detector will achieve better performance than the original tokenized convolutional detector, particularly on tasks that require fine-grained contextual understanding of the internal state. It may encounter challenges in balancing the trade-offs between contextualization and computational efficiency.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Efficient LLM Probing with Tokenized Representations
PROPOSAL: Revise the detector to use hierarchical attention and tree structures, as described in the revised proposal 1. The detector will selectively focus on the most informative regions of the internal state and process the full internal state of an LLM in a hierarchical manner.
CONTROLS: Linear probing classifier as baseline, ablating the attention and tree-based components to compare with traditional single-token probing methods.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised detector will achieve better performance than traditional single-token probing methods, while being computationally efficient enough for real-world deployment. It may struggle with tasks that require fine-grained control over the processing of the internal state.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalizable Hallucination Detection with Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Design a detector that uses contrastive learning to learn a generalizable representation of hallucination across different LLMs and tasks. This detector will be trained on a combination of in-domain and out-of-domain data, and will learn to recognize patterns that are common to hallucinations across different scenarios.
CONTROLS: Training on a mix of in-domain and out-of-domain data, comparing to a standalone detector trained on a single LLM and task.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The detector will significantly improve the generalizability of hallucination detection across different LLMs and tasks, while the quality of the out-of-domain data may affect its performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Cross-Task Transferability of LLM Representations
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability of LLM representations across different tasks and domains. This will involve training multiple detectors on different tasks and measuring their ability to transfer knowledge across these tasks, using both in-domain and out-of-domain data.
CONTROLS: Evaluating transferability across different tasks (e.g. factual question answering, sentiment analysis), ablating the use of shared latent spaces and contrastive learning to understand their contribution.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will reveal the extent to which LLM representations transfer across different tasks and domains, and will highlight the potential benefits and limitations of cross-task knowledge transfer. The transferability of representations may vary significantly across different tasks and datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Hallucination-Specific Features with Causal Masking
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of causal masking to identify features in LLM representations that are specific to hallucinations. This will involve training multiple detectors on different masking patterns and evaluating their ability to detect hallucinations while ignoring non-hallucinatory content.
CONTROLS: Evaluating the impact of different masking patterns on detection performance, comparing to a standard detector trained on the full internal state.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will reveal the existence of characteristic features in LLM representations that are specific to hallucinations, and highlight the potential benefits of causal masking for improved detection performance. The identified features may vary across different LLMs and tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Understanding LLM Hallucinations with Modal-Awareness
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel framework that incorporates modal-awareness into LLM-based hallucination detection, which allows the model to differentiate between hallucinations and non-hallucinatory content by leveraging a separate representation of modal information.
CONTROLS: Comparing to existing hallucination detection methods, investigating the importance of modal-awareness in improving detection performance.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate the benefits of modal-awareness in improving LLM hallucination detection performance, and highlight the challenges and open questions in incorporating this framework into practical applications. The effectiveness of modal-awareness may depend on the quality and accuracy of the modal information available.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Adaptable LLM Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a meta-learning approach that enables the hallucination detector to learn how to adapt to new LLMs, tasks, and domains in a few-shot learning setting. This will involve training a meta-teacher that can generate high-quality hallucination examples for a meta-student to learn from.
CONTROLS: Investigating the impact of few-shot learning, comparing to traditional transfer learning and fine-tuning methods.
COST: 3800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate the effectiveness of meta-learning in enabling adaptable hallucination detection, and highlight the challenges and open questions in meta-learning-based approaches. The adaptability of the detector may vary across different LLMs, tasks, and domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot LLM Hallucination Detection with Multitask Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate a zero-shot learning approach that involves training a hallucination detector to learn the underlying distributions of hallucinations and non-hallucinatory content across multiple tasks and LLMs using multitask learning.
CONTROLS: Comparing to traditional multitask learning methods, investigating the importance of task similarity and LLM similarity in improving zero-shot detection performance.
COST: 4000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The results will demonstrate the feasibility of zero-shot LLM hallucination detection using multitask learning, and highlight the challenges and open questions in this area. The effectiveness of multitask learning may depend on the similarity between tasks and LLMs.

ACTION: ADD
title: propose efficient probing method on internal activations of llms
PROPOSAL: Design a probing classifier that takes in the full 4D internal state of an LLM (layer, token, hidden dimension, batch index) and outputs a probability of hallucination. Utilize a global average pooling (GAP) or spatial mean pooling (SMP) followed by a linear layer or a single linear layer that jointly learns to represent the internal state and predict hallucinations. Regularize the probing model with weight decay and early stopping to prevent overfitting.
CONTROLS: Compare to traditional single-token, single-layer probing and a baseline that uses a separate LLM to detect hallucinations.
COST: estimated 100 GPU hours for 5 LLMs and 3 different probing methods on a synthetic dataset.
PREDICTION: expect moderate improvement over traditional probing methods but may be outperformed by more complex or model-specific approaches. Could fail if the probing method fails to generalize across layers or tokens.

ACTION: ADD
title: dyna-clmp: dynamic CLMP for efficient hallucination detection
PROPOSAL: Extend the correlated layered message passing (CLMP) framework to adaptively select informative positions from the internal state of the LLM. Introduce a dynamics module that predicts the probability of hallucination at each position and selectively attend to those positions with higher probabilities. This adaptive selection process allows the model to efficiently utilize the most informative parts of the internal state while reducing computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original CLMP and a variant that always selects all positions.
COST: estimated 200 GPU hours for 3 LLMs and 3 different scenarios on a synthetic dataset.
PREDICTION: dyna-CLMP will significantly outperform traditional CLMP but may fail if it incorrectly identifies the most informative positions due to limited training data or task-specific characteristics.

ACTION: REVISE
title: extending dyna-clmp to multiple llms: multimodal adaptive probing
PROPOSAL: Revise the previous dyna-CLMP proposal to enable model-agnostic hallucination detection across multiple LLMs. Introduce a multimodal fusion layer that combines the adaptive selection signal from multiple LLMs under a shared probe embedding space. This allows the model to learn a generalized representation of hallucination signals that can be applied to various LLMs on a given task.
CONTROLS: Compare to dyna-CLMP on a single LLM and a baseline that trains a separate probe for each LLM.
COST: estimated 400 GPU hours for 5 LLMs, 2 fusion methods, and 2 different annotation scenarios on a real-world dataset.
PREDICTION: expect moderate improvement over dyna-CLMP when applied to a single LLM and significant improvement when applied to multiple LLMs, but may fail if the LLMs have vastly different architectural designs or activations patterns.

ACTION: REVISE 1
title: global representation modeling for llm hallucination detection
PROPOSAL: Design a probing classifier that takes the entire internal state of an LLM as input and targets a shared representation space for hallucination detection. Train a projection head that maps the high-dimensional internal state to a lower-dimensional space where hallucinations can be effectively detected using a simple linear classifier. Investigate the use of clustering algorithms, autoencoders, or other dimensionality reduction techniques to learn this shared representation.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original proposal 1 and a baseline that uses a fixed, low-dimensional representation space.
COST: estimated 300 GPU hours for 3 LLMs and 2 different clustering methods on a real-world dataset.
PREDICTION: expect significant improvement in hallucination detection accuracy due to the learned shared representation, but may fail if the representation space is not sufficient or is biased towards specific hallucination types.

ACTION: ADD
title: transfer learning for llm hallucination detection
PROPOSAL: Propose a transfer learning framework for LLM hallucination detection that leverages pre-trained probing models and fine-tunes them on new LLMs or tasks. Investigate different transfer learning strategies, such as model pre-training, task adaptation, and few-shot learning. Evaluate the transferability of pre-trained probing models across various LLM architectures, tasks, and domains.
CONTROLS: Compare to training a probing model from scratch for each LLM/task and a baseline that uses a fixed, non-adaptive probing model.
COST: estimated 600 GPU hours for 5 LLMs, 3 transfer learning strategies, and 2 different fine-tuning protocols on a real-world dataset.
PREDICTION: expect significant improvement in transfer learning performance due to the pre-trained probing model knowledge, but may fail if the transfer learning strategy is not effective or if the pre-trained model is not generalizable.

ACTION: ADD
title: self-supervised llm probing with contrastive learning
PROPOSAL: Propose a self-supervised learning framework for LLM hallucination detection based on contrastive learning. Use the internal state of the LLM as anchor and positive samples, and design a negative sampler to generate adversarial representations. Train the probing model to distinguish between anchor-positive and anchor-negative pairs. Evaluate the effect of different negative sampling strategies and contrastive learning objectives on hallucination detection performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to supervised probing on a labeled dataset and a baseline that uses a random negative sampler.
COST: estimated 500 GPU hours for 3 LLMs, 2 different contrastive learning objectives, and 3 negative sampling strategies on a synthetic dataset.
PREDICTION: expect improvement in self-supervised learning performance due to the ability to leverage unlabeled data, but may fail if the negative sampler is not effective or if the contrastive learning objective is not aligned with hallucination detection.

ACTION: ADD
title: calibration of llm probes through probabilistic model of hallucination
PROPOSAL: Model the hallucination detection task as a conditional probability estimation problem, where the goal is to estimate the likelihood of a given output token being a hallucination. Use a probabilistic approach to calibrate the probe's confidence scores, enabling more accurate and reliable hallucination detection. Investigate the use of Bayesian neural networks, probabilistic embeddings, or other probabilistic modeling techniques to improve probe calibration.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard probe calibration methods, such as label smoothing or temperature scaling, and a baseline that uses a non-calibrated probe.
COST: estimated 400 GPU hours for 3 LLMs, 2 different probabilistic models, and 3 calibration methods on a real-world dataset.
PREDICTION: expect improvement in probe calibration and hallucination detection performance due to the probabilistic modeling approach, but may fail if the probabilistic model is not well-specified or if the calibration method is not effective.

action: add
title: evaluating the robustness of llm probes to input transformations
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of different probing methods to input transformations, such as token-level permutation, word shuffling, or synonym substitution. Design a robustness evaluation protocol to assess how probing models generalize to input variations while maintaining their ability to detect hallucinations. Compare the robustness of probing methods proposed in this work (e.g., dyna-CLMP, transfer learning, self-supervised learning, and calibration) and identify which ones are most resilient to input transformations.
CONTROLS: Compare to a set of robustness evaluation baselines using standard probing methods (e.g., traditional CLMP or probing at a single token).
cost: estimated 250 GPU hours for 5 LLMs, 4 different input transformations, and 3 probing methods on a synthetic dataset.
prediction: expect that the most robust probing methods will generalize well to out-of-distribution inputs, but may fail if the input transformations are too drastic or if the probing method is not well-aligned with the task.

action: add
title: dataset partisan effects on llm hallucination detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate the role of dataset partisanship in influencing the performance of LLM hallucination detection probes. Analyze whether probes trained on datasets with biased or partisan data generalizes well to other datasets with different partisanship. Evaluate the robustness of different probing methods to dataset partisanship and assess their potential vulnerabilities to such biases.
CONTROLS: Compare to a set of baseline probing methods that ignore dataset partisanship and a set of probing methods that explicitly account for partisanship in their training.
cost: estimated 400 GPU hours for 5 LLMs, 3 different datasets with varying partisanship, and 4 probing methods on a real-world dataset.
prediction: expect that some probing methods may underperform or fail on datasets with biased partisanship, highlighting the importance of considering data quality and partisanship in mixture across datasets.

action: ADD
title: multi-task learning of hallucination detection and consequence prediction
PROPOSAL: Explore the possibility of training a single LLM probing model to perform not only hallucination detection but also consequence prediction, which aims to identify the risks or consequences associated with each generated output. Investigate the benefits of multi-task learning in improving the performance of both hallucination detection and consequence prediction tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare to training separate probing models for each task using a shared representation and a baseline that uses a single-task probing model for hallucination detection.
COST: estimated 800 GPU hours for 3 LLMs, 2 different multi-task learning methods, and 3 single-task baselines on a real-world dataset.
PREDICTION: expect that multi-task learning will improve the performance of both hallucination detection and consequence prediction tasks, but may fail if the two tasks have conflicting objectives or if the shared representation is not well-learned.

title: investigating full internal state probing for LLM hallucination detection
PROPOSAL: Design a novel, efficient probing classifier that aggregates information from across multiple layer-token pairs, capturing high-level vector relationships between different activations within the LLM's internal state. Specifically, we proposed using a compound directional predictor that derives a unified representation for each activation by computing its dot product with summaries (averages, maximum, or variance) of neighboring activations. This approach favors more interpretable, high-level patterns and promotes transferability across varying model configurations and tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing probing methods (e.g., single-token linear probing, attention-weighted probing), as well as baselines of average and maximum layer-wise encodings. Evaluate model performance on metrics such as detection accuracy, precision, and recall in simulated and real-world settings. Quantify the improvement in detection efficiency (e.g., how many LLM queries per response).
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate higher detection accuracy and generalizability across various model configurations compared to current probing methods. However, actual results might vary based on model variance and the presence of hard hallucination cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: extension to multi-model hallucination detection via shared activations
PROPOSAL: Develop a mid-tier probing framework that captures a shared representation of hallucination patterns across multiple LLMs. To achieve this, we incorporate a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with tailored convolutional kernels suited for detecting patterns within high-dimensional activations. This module identifies similar features that LLMs tend to associate with hallucination, allowing the detector to exploit inter-model relationships and adapt to unseen LLMs.
CONTROLS: Compare this multi-model extension to a single-model variant and model-agnostic attentions-based probing. Assess the trade-off between the detector's performance and adaptation speed on real-world datasets across various domains. Analyze the weakness of this method concerning out-of-distribution (OOD) examples, where hallucinations may diverge between models. Investigate transferability to OOD examples via entropy-level multi-input representations in future iterations.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This novel extension is expected to enhance real-world hallucination detection for lesser-labeled LLMs, given shared hallucination signals. It may exhibit reduced adaptation efficiency concerning encoding variability, and hallucinations of different forms might obscure benefits.
